title: The builder who asks first

beats.say: A client says, build me a house. Do you start laying bricks?
No. A good builder asks questions first. How many people will live there? What is the budget? A design interview works the same way. The prompt is short on purpose, so you must ask.
Then the builder explains each choice. Brick, because it lasts. Not wood, because of fire. They plan for trouble, like burst pipes. And they use numbers: how many rooms, how many square metres.
So interviewers score four things: asking, justifying, planning for failure, and using numbers. There is no single right house.

check.q: Why are design interview prompts kept short on purpose?
opts: To save the interviewer time
To see whether you ask what is needed before building
To hide the right answer tool
To make the round easier
check.why: A vague prompt tests whether you clarify requirements first, which is the first of the four things scored.

work: Before your next project, write three questions you must answer before choosing any tool.
Practise a one-line prompt aloud and ask five clarifying questions before drawing anything.

title: Let the numbers pick the tools

beats.say: Ten million payments a day. Is that a big system or a small one?
Do the maths aloud. A day has about eighty-six thousand seconds. Ten million divided by that is roughly one hundred fifteen events a second. Assume peak is ten times, so about twelve hundred.
If each event is one kilobyte, that is ten gigabytes a day, and about three point six terabytes a year. One modest cluster handles that. You do not need exotic tools.
So the order is: clarify, estimate, draw the boxes, justify each one, then break it on purpose. Numbers decide the tools, not the other way round.

check.q: A system gets 10 million events a day. What is the average rate per second?
opts: About 1,150
About 115
About 11
About 11,500
check.why: 10 million divided by roughly 86,400 seconds is about 115 per second. Peak is a separate multiplier.

work: Memorise that a day is about 86 thousand seconds and a year about 30 million seconds.
For a system you run, write average rate, peak rate and daily storage on one line.

title: Why strong engineers still fail

beats.say: Why do strong engineers still fail design rounds?
Usually they name tools before asking anything. Kafka and Spark in the first minute. The interviewer hears a memorised answer, not a decision.

Second, no rejected alternative. Say why Kafka over a plain queue: replay, and many readers. Third, no failure story. If a consumer dies, it restarts from its saved position, so events may repeat. Writes must be idempotent, meaning safe to run twice.
Finally, check your numbers. Off by a thousand times, and you have picked the wrong architecture.

show.title: Sanity check
items: Is the order of magnitude right?

check.q: A consumer crashes and restarts from its last saved position. What must the sink tolerate?
opts: Lost events
Repeated events
Slower reads
Schema changes
check.why: Restarting from a saved position can replay events, so writes must be idempotent.

work: For each box in a past design, write one rejected alternative and why.
List what happens on component death, late data, and double volume.

title: When the boring answer wins

beats.say: Your design handles a hundred fifteen events a second. Do you really need a streaming platform?
Often not. A queue and a database can carry that load for far less money and far fewer pages at night. Complexity is a cost, paid in people and on-call hours.
So pick one design, and say what would change your mind. If volume grows a hundred times, or latency drops below a second, you move to streaming. Name that trigger aloud.
Depth beats breadth. Spend your time where the risk is, and show you can trade cost, speed and safety on purpose.

show.title: Architect habits
items: Spend time on the riskiest box

check.q: At 115 events a second with relaxed latency, what is the strongest answer?
opts: Full streaming stack for future growth
A simple queue and database, plus a stated trigger to scale
Refuse to answer without more data
List five options without choosing
check.why: Matching complexity to measured load and naming when to change shows senior judgement.

work: Add a 'we would change this if' line to every design you present.
Estimate monthly cost for the simple and the complex version of one design.

title: Why a method beats improvising

beats.say: Why do smart engineers freeze when asked to design a data system in forty-five minutes? Because they start drawing boxes before they know what they are building.

Think of building a house. First you ask the family how many people and what budget. Then you estimate the bricks. Then you sketch the floor plan. Only then do you detail the kitchen and the plumbing.
A design interview works the same way. Ask, do rough math, draw, go deep on two parts, test what breaks, then wrap up. Skipping the questions is like pouring concrete before you know the family size.

check.q: Why ask questions before drawing anything?
opts: It wastes time so the interviewer relaxes
You cannot choose a good design until you know what it must do and how big it is
Drawing is always wrong in interviews
check.why: Requirements and size decide the design. Drawing before knowing them means guessing and probably redoing the work.

work: Before your next design discussion at work, write down three questions about volume, freshness and users.
Practice sketching a pipeline only after listing what must come out of it.

title: The six steps and their minutes

beats.say: How do you spend forty-five minutes so nothing important gets missed?

Clarify for five to eight minutes: what comes in, what goes out, for whom, and how fresh, big and correct it must be. Then estimate for three to five. Fifty thousand events a second at one kilobyte is fifty megabytes a second, about four terabytes a day.

Next, draw the flow for eight to ten minutes: sources, ingest, raw storage, processing, serving, consumers. One sentence per box. Go deep on two components for ten to fifteen. Break it for five. Close in two to three.

check.q: At 50,000 events per second and 1 kilobyte each, roughly how much data arrives per day?
opts: About 4 gigabytes
About 4 terabytes
About 4 petabytes
check.why: 50,000 times 1 kilobyte is 50 megabytes per second. Times 86,400 seconds is about 4.3 terabytes.

work: Memorize the quick conversion: megabytes per second times 86,400 gives daily volume.
Time yourself on a mock design and check you leave five minutes for breaking it.

title: Guarantees, assumptions and the break-it step

beats.say: What do senior candidates say that juniors forget? They state the guarantee out loud.

show.sub: Say it before you are asked

beats.say: For example: dashboards are at most thirty seconds behind and may revise for two minutes; the daily numbers are final. That shows you know late data exists, and when a number stops changing.

Also say your assumptions. If the interviewer stays quiet, announce: I'll assume fifty thousand events per second at peak. An unspoken guess is a hidden risk. Size for the peak, not the average, or you will undersize everything.

show.title: Say it aloud
items: Write it where they can see

beats.say: Then in the break-it step, walk each box. What if it dies? What if events arrive late, or twice? What if traffic grows ten times?

check.q: The interviewer does not answer your question about volume. What should you do?
opts: Wait silently until they answer
Skip estimation entirely
State a number as an assumption, such as 50,000 events per second at peak, and continue
check.why: Stating the assumption keeps you moving and lets the interviewer correct it. Silence or skipping hides the risk.

work: Add a one-line freshness and correctness guarantee to every pipeline design doc.
List assumed peak versus average load in your next capacity estimate.

title: Bending the method like an architect

beats.say: Is a fixed script always right for forty-five minutes? No, and an architect knows where to bend it.

show.sub: Spend time where the risk is

beats.say: Spend the depth where the risk is. If the interviewer cares about correctness, shrink the drawing and go deeper on duplicates and late data. Do not spend ten minutes on a perfect diagram of a simple batch job.

Let the numbers choose the design. Fifty megabytes a second needs only a handful of partitions, but ten times growth needs dozens. If a thirty second delay is acceptable, micro-batches may cost far less than true streaming.
Close by naming what you traded away, such as freshness for cost, and what you would build next.

show.title: Close well
items: Say what you would build next

check.q: The business accepts dashboards being 30 seconds behind. What does that allow?
opts: Cheaper micro-batch processing instead of true streaming
Dropping the raw storage layer
Skipping the failure discussion
check.why: A relaxed freshness target lets you trade latency for lower cost and simpler operations.

work: For each pipeline you own, write the freshness target and ask if a cheaper approach would meet it.
Rehearse a closing statement that names two trade-offs and one next step.

title: The library and the front desk

beats.say: Why would a tiny question freeze your app, when it asks the company's giant data warehouse?

Picture a huge research library. One librarian can spend an hour pulling hundreds of books to answer one deep question. That is a warehouse. It is brilliant at heavy work. But now a thousand people at the door each ask, what time do you open? They queue for hours.

So you add noticeboards at the door. A phone book answers who is this customer, instantly. A live scoreboard answers how many sales this minute. A book index finds a word. Name the question first, then pick the board.

check.q: Thousands of users each ask a small question many times a second. What is the problem with sending them all to the warehouse?
opts: The warehouse cannot store that little data
It handles heavy queries well but many concurrent small ones badly
The answers would be wrong
It only works at night
check.why: Warehouses are built for heavy analytical queries. Thousands of tiny concurrent lookups queue up and cost a lot, so a purpose-built serving store fits better.

work: List the live product features that read from your warehouse today.
For each one, write down the question it asks and how fast it must answer.

title: Key lookups: Redis, DynamoDB, Cassandra

beats.say: How can one lookup come back in a millisecond when you hold a billion records?

Redis keeps data in memory, so a read takes well under a millisecond. It suits counters, sessions, and the latest value per user. DynamoDB and Cassandra use a partition key. The system hashes the key, and the hash picks the machine. So a lookup goes straight to one node and never scans.

Inside a partition, a sort key in DynamoDB, or clustering columns in Cassandra, keep rows in order. So, the last ten orders for user 42, is one ordered read. The catch is you design the table around the query. In Cassandra that means one table per query pattern.

check.q: In DynamoDB, what does the partition key do?
opts: Orders rows inside a partition
Is hashed to decide which node holds the item
Compresses the data
Builds a text index
check.why: The partition key is hashed to pick the node, so a lookup goes straight there. The sort key is what orders items inside it.

work: Write the exact query your feature needs before you choose keys.
Check that your partition key has many distinct values so load spreads.

title: Live analytics and search stores

beats.say: Your dashboard has ten thousand users, each wanting a live count of the last five minutes. Which store survives that?

Pinot, Druid and ClickHouse are columnar. They store each column together, so summing one field reads only that column, not whole rows. They ingest straight from Kafka, so events are queryable within seconds. Uber uses Pinot for user-facing analytics.

Elasticsearch uses an inverted index, a map from each word to the documents holding it. That makes text search and log exploration fast. For complex SQL where seconds are fine, use the warehouse: Snowflake, Redshift, BigQuery, or Trino over the lake.

show.title: Match the pattern
items: Text and logs: Elasticsearch or OpenSearch
Fresh aggregates, many users: Pinot, Druid, ClickHouse
Heavy SQL, seconds fine: the warehouse

check.q: Why does a columnar store sum one field quickly?
opts: It reads only that column, not whole rows
It keeps all data in memory only
It skips the network
It stores one row per node
check.why: Columnar layout keeps each column together, so an aggregate touches only the bytes it needs.

work: Identify dashboards that need fresh data for many concurrent users.
Test one such query on a columnar store and compare latency under load.

title: Where serving stores bite

beats.say: Why does a healthy DynamoDB table throttle at a fraction of its capacity?

Because the hash sends every request for one key to one partition. If a single celebrity user or one date value takes most traffic, that one partition saturates while others sit idle. Pick keys with many distinct values, or add a random suffix to spread the load.

Second gotcha. Tables fit known queries. A new question means a new table, an index, or a backfill. In Cassandra, every table holds a copy, so each write must update all of them. Third, Redis lives in memory. A crash can lose data, so treat it as rebuildable.

show.title: More gotchas
items: New query pattern means new table or backfill
Redis is memory: rebuildable, not the only copy

check.q: A table has a partition key of today's date. What is likely to happen?
opts: Writes spread evenly
All current writes hit one partition and it throttles
Reads become sorted
Nothing, dates are ideal keys
check.why: Every write today shares one key, so one partition takes all the load while the rest idle.

work: Check your busiest partition keys for skew before launch.
Document how each Redis dataset gets rebuilt after a crash.

title: Choosing, and not over-choosing

beats.say: A team wants one store to serve everything. Why does that plan fail?

Each store optimises one access pattern. So name the pattern first: latency, request rate, freshness, and concurrency. Redis memory costs far more per gigabyte than disk, so keep only latest values, with expiry. Warehouses bill for compute, so thousands of small queries burn money and still queue.

Often the best move is to precompute. Let the stream job write finished answers into DynamoDB or Redis. Use Pinot or ClickHouse only when users slice fresh data freely. If data is small, plain Postgres may do. Cassandra scales writes but needs real operations skill.

check.q: Users only ever need a fixed set of numbers per customer, updated continuously. What is the best design?
opts: Query the warehouse on each page load
Precompute in the stream job and serve from a key-value store
Use Elasticsearch for everything
Scan Kafka on demand
check.why: The question is known, so precomputed results in a key-value store give the cheapest, fastest lookups. Ad hoc engines are needed only when users slice freely.

work: Write a one-page access-pattern table before approving any new store.
Cost out memory, compute, and operations for your top two choices.

title: The AI feature is a new teammate

beats.say: If the interviewer says add AI to this system, what are you really adding? Think of it as hiring a very fast, very confident new teammate.
You would not hand them the keys on day one. You decide which files they can see, how you will check their work, and how much time and money each task may take.
You also decide what they may change, and when a person must sign off. And you keep a diary of everything they did, so a bad answer can be explained.

check.q: An interviewer asks you to add an AI feature to an existing system. What is the strongest first move?
opts: Treat the model as a component with its own context, evaluation, budgets, guardrails and tracing
Choose the largest available model, because higher quality removes most other concerns
Let the model write straight to the database so there is no extra step to maintain
Launch quickly and add request tracing later, once users report bad answers
check.why: The model is one more component with its own requirements: what data it needs, how quality is measured, latency and cost limits, what it may change, and a trace to explain answers. A bigger model fixes none of those.

work: List context, evaluation, budget, guardrails and tracing for any AI feature before you build it.
Decide which actions the model may never take without a person approving.

title: RAG at a thousand questions a second: the sums

beats.say: How big is the bill for answering a thousand questions every second? Do the sums before you draw any boxes.

Ten million documents of two thousand tokens, cut into chunks of five hundred, make about forty million chunks. Each vector is four kilobytes, so the index is about one hundred sixty gigabytes. Quantised to int8 it is about forty. So shard it four ways and replicate each shard.

A thousand questions a second is eighty-six million a day. At two thousand input tokens each, that is about one hundred seventy billion tokens. Assuming twenty cents per million, input alone costs about thirty-five thousand dollars a day. That number drives the design.

check.q: Why does the estimate come before the architecture in the retrieval design?
opts: Daily token cost and index size shape which caches, shards and models you need
Interviewers prefer numbers to boxes, so the order is purely a matter of style
The index must be built first because the prompt cannot be sized without it
Token prices are fixed quotes, so the bill can be read straight off a price list
check.why: About 40 GB to 160 GB of vectors forces sharding and replicas, and roughly $35,000 a day of input tokens forces caching and routing. Prices are assumptions you state, not quotes.

work: Practice estimating chunks, index size and daily tokens on a whiteboard in under two minutes.
Always state your assumed price per million tokens before giving a cost.

title: Where the first second goes

beats.say: Where do the first one and a half seconds go in a retrieval answer?

The question passes the gateway and is embedded. Hybrid search then runs, vector plus keyword, filtered by what this user may see. A cross-encoder reranks the top fifty. The prompt is built with numbered passages.

Gateway ten milliseconds, embedding twenty, retrieval fifty, reranking a hundred, prompt ten. Then the model takes five hundred to eight hundred before the first word. The model is the budget, so everything else must stay small. Then the answer streams.

check.q: In the latency budget, which stage dominates time to the first token?
opts: The model's time to first token, so the other stages must stay small
The rerank step, because cross-encoders are the slowest part of any search
The retrieval step, since scanning forty million chunks is always the slowest
The gateway, because identity and quota checks run before everything else
check.why: The model takes 500 to 800 ms, while the gateway, embedding, retrieval, rerank and prompt add up to about 190 ms. Streaming lets the user see words while the rest generates.

work: Write a per-stage p95 budget for any AI request and check it in tracing.
Stream model output so users see the first words early.

title: Reviewing code an assistant wrote

beats.say: An assistant wrote your pipeline in two minutes, and it runs. So what could possibly be wrong?

show.sub: Flaws hide in behaviour over time

beats.say: One real example overwrote the full history on every run, re-scored rows that had not changed, and averaged all of history when the business wanted a recent window.

show.title: Three hidden flaws
items: Averaged all time, not a recent window

beats.say: Ask five questions. What happens on the second run, and the hundredth? Does it process only what changed? Does it compute the grain and window asked for? What does a run cost as data grows? And how does it treat duplicates, late data and nulls?

check.q: A generated pipeline passes its first test run. Which review question finds the most serious hidden risk?
opts: What happens on the second and hundredth run, and what does each cost?
Does the code use the same naming style as the rest of the repository?
Did the assistant add comments explaining every function it wrote?
Does the pipeline finish quickly on the small sample used for testing?
check.why: Generated code usually runs once. Problems appear over time: full overwrites, reprocessing unchanged rows and growing cost. Style and sample speed reveal none of that.

work: Run any generated pipeline twice and compare outputs and cost.
Check the metric against the business window and grain before approving.

title: Refund once, never twice

beats.say: A support agent says your refund is on its way. What stops it paying twice?

It is one agent with a few tools, not several, because the task does not split into independent parts. Refunds and cancels are jobs on a queue, each with an idempotency key. That is a unique label, so a retry is recognised and does not act again. The agent replies at once while a worker does the slow part.
The limit lives in the refund tool, not the prompt. The tool checks the amount and that the customer owns the order. Above the limit, a person approves.
Customer text is data, never instructions, and the agent can only call tools it was given. That limits prompt injection.

show.title: Injection defence
items: Only granted tools can be called

check.q: Where should the refund limit and order ownership checks be enforced?
opts: Inside the refund tool itself, whatever the model asks for
In the system prompt, telling the model never to exceed the limit
In the chat window, by hiding the refund button from customers
In the evaluation set, which will catch any bad refund afterwards
check.why: Prompts can be talked around by injected text. A tool that enforces limits and ownership holds no matter what the model asks. Evals measure risk but do not prevent it.

work: Move every business rule from the prompt into the tool that acts.
Give each write action an idempotency key and test a double retry.

title: Leaks, inventions and failures in RAG

beats.say: Your search is fast and your answers sound great. So how might it leak secrets or invent facts?
Permissions are stored with each chunk and filtered during retrieval. If you filter after the model has read it, it is already too late.
To limit wrong answers, answer only from retrieved passages, cite them, and say I do not know when the retrieval score is low. Measure groundedness on a golden set before every change.

show.title: Fewer wrong answers
items: I do not know below a score

beats.say: Plan for failure. If the provider throttles, use the cache or a second provider. If a shard dies, replicas serve. After a deploy empties the cache, warm it. And re-embed only changed chunks.

check.q: Where must document permissions be applied in a retrieval pipeline?
opts: During retrieval, so forbidden chunks never reach the model
After the answer is written, by removing sentences the user cannot see
At login only, since a signed-in user may read every indexed chunk
In the system prompt, by asking the model to respect access rules
check.why: Once forbidden text is in the prompt it can leak into the answer. Storing permissions with each chunk and filtering at search time keeps it out entirely.

work: Store access labels on every chunk and test with a user who has no access.
Build a golden set and run groundedness before each prompt or model change.

title: Cutting the thirty-five thousand dollar bill

beats.say: Thirty-five thousand dollars a day for input tokens alone. Where do you cut it?

Three levers. A semantic cache returns a stored answer when a new question is very close to an old one; support traffic often hits thirty to sixty percent. Routing easy questions to a small model is the second. Caching the fixed system prompt is the third.
Each has a price. A cache can serve stale answers, and a small model can be wrong more often. So prove every lever on your evaluation set, and say your price assumptions out loud.

check.q: You add a semantic cache and a small-model router. What must you do before keeping them?
opts: Check on the evaluation set that quality holds while cost falls
Assume savings are safe, since cached answers were once correct
Remove the evaluation set, because the cache replaces model calls
Route every question to the small model so savings are maximal
check.why: Both levers trade quality for cost: caches can be stale and small models err more. Only an evaluation set shows whether the savings are worth it.

work: Measure cache hit rate and answer quality on cache hits separately.
Add an escalation path from small to large model when confidence is low.

title: Why one gateway for every model call

beats.say: Why force every team through one gateway instead of letting them call providers directly?

Teams never hold provider keys. The gateway applies a token bucket quota per team, a monthly budget, allowed models and redaction of personal data. Every call is traced with tokens, cost, latency and team, so spend is reported per team.

It checks caches, then a router sends easy tasks to a small model and escalates when unsure. If a provider fails, it retries and fails over to a second provider or region. Batch work uses cheaper batch APIs.

chip.text: Outage does not stop the company

check.q: What is the main benefit of a central gateway over direct provider calls from each team?
opts: Shared keys, quotas, budgets, tracing and failover are handled in one place
It removes provider rate limits, since the gateway has unlimited capacity
It guarantees the cheapest model answers every request without routing
It lets each team set its own policies and never coordinate spend
check.why: A gateway keeps keys out of teams' hands and centralises quotas, budgets, redaction, caching, routing, tracing and failover. It does not remove provider limits or choose models without a router.

work: Give each team a quota and budget and report spend per team from traces.
Set up failover to a second provider and test it with a simulated outage.

title: The cut phone line

beats.say: What should a bank branch do when its phone line to head office is cut?
Two branches share one ledger. The line goes down, so neither sees the other's changes. This cut is called a partition.
Option one: refuse withdrawals until the line returns. Every balance is correct, but some customers are turned away. That is choosing consistency.
Option two: keep serving, using the last balance you know. Nobody waits, but a number might be stale. That is choosing availability.
You only have to choose during the cut. When the line works, you get both.

check.q: A store keeps answering during a network partition, even though some answers may be stale. What did it choose?
opts: Consistency
Availability
Neither; that is impossible
Durability
check.why: Answering with possibly stale data during a partition is the availability choice. Refusing requests would be the consistency choice.

work: For each data store you own, write down whether it refuses or answers stale during a partition.
Ask which of your user actions can tolerate a stale answer and which cannot.

title: Why a crowd crushes a recovering server

beats.say: Why does a shop that reopens after a power cut sometimes get crushed again within seconds?
Everyone who was waiting rushes in at the same moment. A server that just recovered is fragile, and thousands of clients retrying together can knock it flat again.
The fix is polite waiting. After each failure, wait longer: one second, then two, then four. That is exponential backoff, meaning the wait doubles.
Add jitter, which means randomness. Each client waits a slightly different time, so the crowd trickles in instead of arriving as one wave.

check.q: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
opts: So each retry waits longer
So clients stop retrying sooner
So clients do not all retry at the same instant
So the server can ignore duplicates
check.why: Without randomness, clients that failed together keep retrying in sync. Jitter spreads them out.

work: Check what wait time your clients use between retries.
Add randomness to any fixed retry delay.

title: Quorums with real numbers

beats.say: Three copies of your data, and one is down. How can a read still be right?
Say N is three replicas. A write waits for W copies to confirm; set W to two. A read asks R copies; set R to two.
Any two groups of two out of three must share at least one copy. So the read always touches a replica holding the latest write.
The rule is that R plus W must be bigger than N. Here two plus two is four, bigger than three.
Want faster reads? Set R to one and W to three. Reads are quick, but every write needs all replicas.

check.q: With N=5 replicas and W=3, what is the smallest R that guarantees overlap?
check.why: R + W must exceed N. With W=3 and N=5, R must be greater than 2, so R=3. Option 2 gives 2+3=5, which is not greater than 5.

work: Write down N, R and W for your main replicated store.
Check whether it can serve reads when one replica is down.

title: Why a ring beats mod N

beats.say: You add a fourth server to a cluster of three. Should most of your data move?
With simple hashing, the server is the key's hash mod the node count. Change three to four and about three quarters of keys land somewhere new. That is a huge reshuffle.
Consistent hashing puts servers and keys on a ring. Each key belongs to the next server clockwise.

chip.text: Key goes to next node clockwise

beats.say: Add a server and it takes over only the slice just before it. With four nodes, roughly one quarter of keys move.
Hash partitioning spreads load evenly but makes range scans hit every node. Range partitioning keeps neighbours together, but a hot range can overload one node.

show.title: Partitioning trade
items: Hash: even load, costly range scans

check.q: Why is consistent hashing preferred over hash mod N when nodes are added?
opts: It makes range scans cheap
Only a small share of keys move
It removes the need for replicas
It guarantees no hot keys
check.why: On a ring, a new node only takes over a slice of one neighbour's keys. Mod N changes the owner of most keys.

work: Find out how your store assigns keys to nodes.
Estimate how much data would move if you added one node.

title: Retry storms and how to stop them

beats.say: Your service dies at noon and recovers at one minute past. Why does it die again?
Ten thousand clients failed, waited a fixed second, and retried together. Each wave arrives in sync, so load spikes instead of spreading.
Backoff alone does not fix it. If everyone doubles together, they still collide at one, two, four seconds. Jitter breaks the sync, by picking a random wait up to the current cap.

show.title: Backoff needs jitter
items: Jitter: random wait up to the cap

beats.say: Also cap the retries and the maximum wait, or a long outage multiplies traffic. And retry only safe calls: a repeated payment needs an idempotency key, so it applies once.

check.q: Clients use exponential backoff with no jitter. What problem remains?
opts: Waits never grow
Clients that failed together still retry together
Requests can never succeed
Servers cannot recover
check.why: Identical doubling keeps clients synchronized, so spikes recur at each step. Randomness breaks the synchronization.

work: Audit retry code for caps on attempts and total wait.
Confirm that retried write calls carry an idempotency key.

title: What quorums and CAP do not promise

beats.say: If R plus W exceeds N, are reads guaranteed correct? Not quite.
Overlap only promises that one replica you read has the newest copy. The client must still pick it, usually by timestamp or version. Clock skew can pick the wrong one.
Sloppy quorums, which write to stand-in nodes during failures, break the overlap until hints are handed back. A write that fails halfway can also leave partial copies that later reads see.
And CAP is about partitions only. Without one, the real trade is latency against consistency: waiting for more replicas is slower.

show.sub: More replicas waited on, slower answer

check.q: Which situation can break the guarantee that R + W > N reads see the latest write?
opts: A sloppy quorum writing to stand-in nodes
Using three replicas
Setting R equal to W
Reading from the leader
check.why: Stand-in nodes mean the write may not sit on the replicas the read later asks, so the overlap argument no longer holds.

work: Find out if your store uses sloppy quorums or hinted handoff.
Check how it resolves conflicting versions on reads.

title: Region failure: RPO and RTO

beats.say: A whole region goes dark. What two numbers does your design owe the business?
RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data you can lose, measured in time. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long you can be down.

show.title: Two targets
items: RPO: data you can lose, in time

beats.say: Asynchronous replication to another region gives an RPO of seconds and keeps writes fast. Synchronous replication gives an RPO of zero, but every write pays cross-region latency.
RTO depends on the standby. Restoring backups takes hours, a warm standby minutes, active-active near zero, at roughly double the cost.
Pick targets from the business cost of loss, then buy only that.

show.text: Price the loss, then buy the target

check.q: The business says losing even one committed transaction on region failure is unacceptable. What does that set?
opts: RTO of zero
RPO of zero
Both are unconstrained
A quorum of one
check.why: RPO measures data loss in time. No loss means RPO zero, which generally requires synchronous replication across regions.

work: Write RPO and RTO into the design doc for every critical system.
Test a failover and record the real recovery time.

title: Choosing stale or strict on purpose

beats.say: When would you choose a store that may serve stale data on purpose?
When being up matters more than being exact: shopping carts, feeds, sensor events. Use Cassandra or DynamoDB, with quorum reads for the requests that need them.
When money or inventory must be exact, choose a single-leader relational database. Refusing a request in a partition is cheaper than double-selling a seat.
The partition key matters too. Hash for even load and point lookups. Range if reports scan time windows, but split the hot recent range.
Tune per request, not per company.

check.q: Which workload is the best fit for a single-leader relational database rather than an availability-first store?
opts: Social media feed
Seat booking with limited inventory
Sensor event ingest
Shopping cart suggestions
check.why: Limited inventory must not be double-sold, so refusing during a partition is better than serving stale data.

work: Classify each data domain as must-be-exact or can-be-stale.
Choose partition keys by checking real query patterns and hot-spot risk.

title: A day of events is just a tap

beats.say: A company gets one hundred billion events a day. Is that huge, or just a busy tap?

show.sub: scary, or just a busy tap?

beats.say: Here is the trick. A day has about eighty-six thousand seconds, so call it one hundred thousand. Divide the day's total by that, and you get a rate per second. One hundred billion becomes about a million a second.
Think of a tap filling a bath. The tap is the rate per second. The bath is the total stored. Pipes must handle the tap, and the bath size sets your storage bill.
Once you have those two numbers, everything else is multiplying. Size of one event times the rate gives the flow. Flow times time gives storage.

show.title: Everything else is *multiplying*
items: Event size times rate gives flow
Storage times price gives the bill

check.q: A system gets 100 billion events a day. About what rate must it handle each second?
opts: About 1.2 million events per second
About 100 million events per second
About 12,000 events per second
check.why: A day has about 86,400 seconds, so 100 billion divided by that is roughly 1.2 million per second. The other answers are off by factors of about a hundred.

work: Convert any daily volume into per second by dividing by about 100,000 before you design anything.
Write down event size, rate and retention, then multiply them to get flow and storage.

title: One million events a second, sized

beats.say: A million events a second. How many Kafka partitions is that?

At one kilobyte each, that is one gigabyte a second, or about eighty-six terabytes a day raw. One partition takes roughly four megabytes a second. So one gigabyte divided by four megabytes is two hundred fifty partitions. Plan three to five hundred for peak and headroom.
Replication factor three triples the writes, so the cluster writes about three gigabytes a second to disk. Brokers take a few hundred megabytes a second each, so you need at least ten brokers.
Stored as Parquet, ten times smaller, it is about ten terabytes a day. That is three point six petabytes a year, around eighty thousand dollars a month of standard storage.

show.title: Raw versus *Parquet* per day
items: 3.6 PB a year, about $80k a month

check.q: Ingest is 1 GB/s and one partition takes about 4 MB/s. What is a sensible partition plan?
opts: About 300 to 500 partitions, for headroom
About 25 partitions, since Kafka is fast
About 4,000 partitions, one per MB of flow
check.why: One gigabyte divided by four megabytes is 250. Add headroom for peaks of two to three times and growth, giving 300 to 500. Twenty-five is far too few, and 4,000 is wasteful.

work: Do the partition division out loud in design reviews: total MB/s over per-partition MB/s.
Multiply replication factor into disk and network estimates, not just the incoming rate.

title: Turn per terabyte into per month

beats.say: How much do your dashboards cost per month? Most people never turn a price per terabyte into a monthly bill.
Two thousand queries an hour, each scanning fifty gigabytes. That is one hundred terabytes an hour. At five dollars a terabyte, that is five hundred dollars an hour.
Over a month that is about three hundred sixty thousand dollars.

Now partition by date and cluster by the filter column, so each query reads one gigabyte. That is fifty times less. A daily summary table that dashboards read instead cuts it again. Always say the monthly number out loud.

check.q: Dashboards scan 50 GB per query on an unpartitioned table in a pay-per-TB warehouse. What is the best first fix?
opts: Partition by date and cluster by the filter column
Buy a bigger warehouse so each query finishes faster
Cache the results in the browser for each user
check.why: Cost follows bytes scanned, so cutting the bytes each query reads cuts the bill. A faster warehouse does not reduce bytes scanned, and browser caching does not help most queries.

work: Translate every per-TB price into dollars per month before approving a query pattern.
Check bytes scanned per dashboard query and add partition filters or a daily aggregate table.

title: Where the numbers bite: S3 and peaks

beats.say: You write twenty thousand objects a second to S3 and many requests fail. Why?

S3 allows about thirty-five hundred writes a second per prefix, a prefix being the key path before the file name. Twenty thousand under one prefix gets throttled. Spread keys over at least six prefixes, and more for headroom.

Small files hurt too. Millions of tiny files mean millions of requests, at five dollars per million writes, and slow query planning. Aim for one hundred twenty-eight megabytes to one gigabyte per file.

show.title: Aim for *big* files
items: Target 128 MB to 1 GB per file
Millions of tiny files mean millions of requests
Query planning slows as file counts grow

beats.say: And always plan for peak. Average is not enough. Size for two to three times the average, or a spike will back up your pipeline.

check.q: 20,000 object writes a second all go under one S3 prefix. What happens and what is the fix?
opts: Writes beyond about 3,500 a second throttle; spread keys over more prefixes
S3 scales one prefix without limit; add more writer threads
Writes slow only for large files; compact files into bigger ones
check.why: Each prefix supports roughly 3,500 writes a second, so extra writes get throttled. More prefixes add more rate. Adding threads or compacting does not raise the per-prefix limit.

work: Compute requests per second per prefix before choosing a key layout for high-volume writes.
Compact small files to 128 MB or more and size capacity for two to three times average load.

title: Losing a region: RPO and RTO

beats.say: If a whole region dies, how much data do you lose?
Two numbers answer that. RPO is how much data you can lose, measured in time. RTO is how long you can be down. Say them first, before drawing anything.

show.title: State the *targets* first
items: RPO: how much data loss is acceptable, in time
RTO: how long an outage is acceptable
Agree both before drawing the design

beats.say: Asynchronous replication between regions adds fifty to one hundred fifty milliseconds plus any backlog. So RPO is seconds, never zero. Zero needs synchronous writes, which pay that delay on every single write.

Two regions taking writes also conflict. Pin each key to a home region, or use last writer wins with trusted clocks, or counters that merge safely. And replicating ten terabytes a day costs about two hundred dollars a day.

show.title: Resolve *conflicts*
items: Home region per key, users pinned
Last writer wins, only with trusted clocks
10 TB a day across regions costs about $200

check.q: Two regions replicate asynchronously and one fails. What is true about data loss?
opts: Recent writes still in the replication backlog may be lost
No data is lost, since both regions hold every write
Only data older than the last daily backup is lost
check.why: Asynchronous replication lags by network delay plus backlog, so the newest writes may not have arrived. Zero loss needs synchronous writes. Daily backups are not what limits loss here.

work: Write RPO and RTO numbers into every multi-region design before choosing the technology.
Pick a conflict rule per dataset, such as a home region per key, and cost the inter-region transfer.

title: Backfill: pay per terabyte or run your own

beats.say: Reprocessing three years of data. Pay per terabyte, or run your own cluster?
Seven and a half petabytes raw is about one and a half as Parquet. Scanned at five dollars a terabyte, that is seven thousand five hundred dollars a pass, and a bug means paying again.
Your own Spark reads about fifty megabytes a second per core. That is roughly eight thousand three hundred core-hours. About four hundred dollars on demand, or one hundred forty on spot.
So compute is cheap, and per terabyte scanning is not. Make the backfill idempotent and run it partition by partition on spot, because a reclaimed machine then just reruns one slice.

show.title: Design the *backfill*
items: Compute is cheap, per-TB scanning is not
Spot nodes can vanish, so reruns must be safe
Spread S3 keys over prefixes for writes

check.q: You must recompute 1.5 PB of Parquet and may need to rerun after bugs. What is the best choice?
opts: Own Spark on spot, with idempotent partition-by-partition jobs
A pay-per-TB engine, since it needs no cluster to run
Own Spark on demand only, since spot is too risky
check.why: Own compute costs hundreds of dollars a pass against thousands for per-TB scanning. Idempotent partition jobs make lost spot machines harmless. On demand costs about three times more with no gain.

work: Estimate a backfill both ways, per-TB scan versus vCPU-hours, before choosing an engine.
Make jobs idempotent by partition so spot loss and reruns are cheap.

title: Let the numbers justify the design

beats.say: Three thousand events a second. Do you really need Kafka?
Three thousand a second at one kilobyte is three megabytes a second. One database can take that write load, so Kafka adds machines and on-call work for nothing.
Now a million a second. That is a gigabyte a second, so you need hundreds of partitions, and a single database cannot absorb it. Here Kafka earns its place.
The interviewer rarely checks your arithmetic. They check that you did it, and that your design follows from it.

show.title: Show the *method*
items: Multiply to flow, storage and cost
Pick the design the numbers justify

check.q: At 3,000 events per second, what should you say about proposing Kafka?
opts: Justify it, since one database could take that load
Use it, since every pipeline needs a message queue
Avoid it, since Kafka tops out below 10,000 events a second
check.why: Three MB/s is within one database's reach, so Kafka needs a reason such as replay or many consumers. Kafka is not mandatory, and it scales far beyond 10,000 events a second.

work: Open every design answer with rate, event size and retention, then show the multiplication.
For each component you add, name the number that forces it.

title: Fast guess, final count

beats.say: Why does a news channel call an election at nine at night, yet the official result takes days?
The channel counts a sample of ballots. That is quick, but it can be wrong. The election office counts every single ballot, slowly, and its number is final.
Data systems split the job the same way. A stream gives a dashboard number within seconds. A nightly batch recounts everything, including late arrivals.
Use the fast number to watch. Use the final number to bill. When they disagree, the final one wins.

check.q: A dashboard shows 1,000 orders at noon but the nightly batch says 1,040. What most likely happened?
opts: Late events arrived after the stream had already counted
The batch job double counted orders by mistake
The dashboard is always the more accurate number
Someone changed the order data after midnight
check.why: Streams report what has arrived so far. Late events show up only when the batch recounts, so the batch is the final number.

work: List which of your dashboards show early numbers and which show final ones.
Label each metric as estimate or final so readers know which to trust.
Pick one number that drives money and make sure it comes from the final recount.

title: Erasing one name from a giant library

beats.say: A customer says, erase everything you know about me. Your company has a petabyte of files. Where do you even start?
Picture a giant library where her name is written on pages inside millions of books. Searching every book for every request would take forever.

show.title: Her name is on *millions* of pages

chip.text: One search per request is too slow

beats.say: So the librarian keeps a list of names to erase. Once a week, a team goes through the shelves once and rewrites only the pages that mention anyone on the list.
Old copies in the archive room must be thrown away too. Otherwise her name still exists, and the law gives you only thirty days.

check.q: Why batch many deletion requests into one weekly pass?
opts: Each pass rewrites many files, so doing it once saves work
The law requires deletions to happen only on weekends
Batching makes the erased data recoverable later on
A single request cannot be found without other requests
check.why: Rewriting files is costly. One weekly pass handles every request together and still meets the 30 day deadline.

work: Write down every place a person's data can live.
Keep one list of deletion requests with dates.
Check that the weekly pass finishes well inside thirty days.

title: Remembering impressions for a click

beats.say: Fifty billion ad impressions a day. How much memory does it take to wait for a click?
Fifty billion a day is about six hundred thousand a second. A click can arrive hours after its impression, so the stream job must remember each impression for a day.
Say each one takes one hundred bytes. Six hundred thousand times eighty-six thousand seconds times one hundred bytes is about five terabytes of state.
Shrink each record to a twenty byte key and it drops to about one terabyte. Or skip the stream join, and join in batch, where disk is cheap.

check.q: Why does the click-to-impression stream join need so much state?
opts: Every impression must wait in memory in case a click arrives
Each click needs to be copied to every partition twice
The join stores all conversions from the past seven days
Kafka keeps a full copy of each record inside the job
check.why: Impressions come first and clicks later, so every impression is held for the window. Volume times window times size gives the state.

work: Estimate state as rate times window times bytes per record before building any join.
Store only the fields attribution needs.
Compare a batch join against the stream join for cost.

title: The weekly delete pipeline

beats.say: How do you delete one person from a petabyte lake without rewriting the whole lake?
First, every request goes into a deletion log, keyed by user id. Every table keeps the user id in each row, so we can find the rows.
Once a week, one job deletes all the logged ids together. In merge on read mode, this only marks rows as deleted. It is fast, but the bytes are still on disk.
Then compaction rewrites the affected files without those rows, and snapshot expiry removes the old files. Rewriting one percent of a petabyte is ten terabytes of reads and writes a week.

check.q: After a merge on read delete runs, why is the person's data not yet gone?
opts: Rows are only marked, so files and old snapshots still hold them
The delete skips rows older than seven days by design
Compaction runs first and restores the marked rows again
The deletion log keeps the table from being queried
check.why: Deletion vectors hide rows from queries. Only compaction and snapshot expiry remove the bytes.

work: Run delete, compaction and snapshot expiry as one scheduled workflow.
Estimate the weekly rewrite cost from the share of files affected.
Confirm user id is a column in every table that holds personal data.

title: Is the delete really a delete?

beats.say: You ran the delete. The query returns nothing. Is the person really gone?
Not yet. A delete marker hides the row from queries, but the original file still holds it. Compaction must rewrite that file.
Even then, table snapshots keep old versions for time travel. Until snapshot expiry runs, anyone can query last week's table and see the person.
Check the other copies too. Kafka topics expire after seven days. Backups, caches and exports need to follow the same deletion log. Keep proof, because auditors will ask.

check.q: Compaction finished, but last week's snapshot is still queryable. What is the risk?
opts: Time travel can still read the person's old rows
The compacted files will be rewritten back again
Queries on today's table will return the person
The deletion log entry will be removed too early
check.why: Old snapshots point at old files. Until snapshot expiry removes them, the data is still readable and the deletion is not complete.

work: Test deletion end to end: after expiry, try to read the user through time travel.
Set snapshot retention shorter than the legal deadline.
Add backups and exports to the deletion runbook.

title: Fail open or fail closed

beats.say: A card payment waits on your fraud model. The model is slow today. Do you block the payment or let it through?
The payment has a budget, say one hundred milliseconds. Scoring reads precomputed features, like swipes in the last ten minutes, from a fast store that a stream job keeps fresh.
If scoring times out, a fallback rule decides. Fail open lets it through and risks fraud. Fail closed blocks it and annoys honest customers. Choose by amount and risk.
Chargebacks arrive weeks later, so labels for training are late. Log every decision and feature to the lake so you can learn from them.

check.q: The scoring service times out on a small payment. What should the design have ready?
opts: A fallback rule that decides within the latency budget
A retry loop that keeps waiting until the model answers
A queue that holds the payment until the next morning
A rule that always blocks any payment that is slow
check.why: Payments must not wait. A defined fallback decides inside the budget, and open or closed is chosen by risk.

work: Set a timeout and an explicit fallback for each payment amount band.
Split features into those that need streaming freshness and those that can be batch.
Log the features used for every decision so later training matches what the model saw.

title: Why bill from the slower pipeline

beats.say: Why would a company bill advertisers from a slower pipeline than the one on its dashboard?

show.text: Stream to watch, batch to bill

beats.say: Conversions can arrive seven days after a click. A stream has already moved on, so its numbers are early guesses.

chip.text: Arrives too late for the stream

beats.say: A daily batch looks back seven days, recomputes last-click attribution, and restates the affected days. Billing uses these numbers because money needs the final answer.
The cost is two pipelines to run, and dashboard numbers that later shift. The trade is worth it when spend errors reach invoices. If nobody bills from it, run only the stream.

show.title: The trade-off
items: Worth it when invoices depend on it
No billing? Stream alone may do

check.q: Why does billing use the batch numbers and not the stream's?
opts: Batch sees late conversions and restates days to final values
Batch is cheaper per record, so invoices cost less to make
The stream cannot read the impressions topic in Kafka
Advertisers prefer numbers computed once a day anyway
check.why: Conversions arrive up to seven days late. Only a lookback batch can include them, so only it gives final numbers.

work: Name which metrics are estimates and which are final, and who may bill from each.
Publish a restatement window so finance knows when numbers settle.
Reconcile stream totals against batch totals daily and alert on drift.

title: Compute per-user once, not per experiment

beats.say: Two thousand experiments run at once. Why does joining raw events for each one break your cluster?
Each join scans billions of exposure and metric events. Two thousand experiments means scanning the same events two thousand times.
Instead, build a per-user metric table once a day, then every experiment joins its small exposure list to it. The cost no longer grows with raw events per experiment.
Assignment is a hash of user and experiment id, so no lookup is needed. Check sample ratio mismatch first, because a skewed split makes every result suspect.

show.title: Guard the results
items: Assign by hashing user and experiment
Log exposure when the change is seen
Track guardrail metrics on every test

check.q: What is the main reason to precompute a per-user metric table?
opts: Raw events are scanned once, not once for every experiment
It removes the need to log exposures for each user
It lets each user be placed in only a single experiment
Per-user totals make confidence intervals unnecessary
check.why: Scanning raw events is the expensive step. Doing it once and reusing the result keeps cost flat as experiments grow.

work: Build shared per-user metric tables and have every experiment reuse them.
Add a sample ratio mismatch check as the first step of every result.
Set guardrail metrics that every test must report.
